Yes — it is coherent to say that a person can be harmed by an event after death, but only in a qualified sense.

My view is that death does not automatically end all possible interests a person had while alive. Some interests can extend beyond death: not necessarily because the dead person is still “experiencing” anything, but because what happens after death can still frustrate aims, commitments, and expectations that belonged to the person when alive. On that view, the breaking of a promise made to someone can count as a harm to them even if the breach occurs after death, because the wrong is measured against the person’s standing interests and projects, not just their present sensations.

That said, this is not harm in the same way as pain, fear, or deprivation experienced while alive. It is a non-experiential harm: a failure to honor an obligation that existed in relation to that person. So the claim is coherent if we distinguish:
- **experienced harms**, which require a living subject of experience, and
- **interest-based or status-based harms**, which can survive death insofar as the person’s prior interests, wishes, or claims are implicated.

### What this implies about wills
This view strongly supports the moral significance of wills. A will is not just a dead letter; it is an instrument through which a person’s posthumous interests are expressed. If posthumous harms are possible, then disregarding a valid will can wrong the deceased, not merely inconvenience the living. That gives weight to testamentary freedom and to duties to carry out one’s final instructions.

But it does not imply that every wish a person had must be obeyed forever. Some wishes may be weak, conflicting, or overridden by stronger moral or legal considerations. Still, in general, a will should be treated as more than a practical recommendation; it is a way a person can continue to shape how they are treated after death.

### What this implies about posthumous reputation
It also implies that posthumous reputation matters morally, not just socially. If a dead person can be harmed by later events, then false accusations, malicious distortions, or public humiliation after death can wrong them in some sense. Their reputation becomes part of what survives them: not as a conscious possession, but as an extension of how their life and projects are recognized.

At the same time, this should not be overstated. Dead people do not suffer embarrassment or distress in the ordinary psychological sense. So posthumous reputation is morally important because it concerns honor, memory, and the fulfillment of the person’s standing interests, not because the dead literally feel insulted.

### Bottom line
So, yes: it is coherent to say a person can be harmed after death, if harm is understood as the frustration of interests, promises, or claims that outlast death. That makes wills morally weighty and gives real moral significance to posthumous reputation, while still recognizing that the dead are not harmed by postmortem events in the same experiential way the living are.
